steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite moves around the screen? 

❓ What might be added to improve the User Experience (UX) of this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to both play the project and review the starter code. Prompt the ninja to notice that there is already a tilemap and several different types of sprites (Player, Key, Artifact, Enemy) on screen. The Key sprite is required in order to “unlock” the museum to collect the Artifact sprites.

💡 In this activity, the ninja will explore adding the Raycasting extension to improve the project’s User Experience (UX). The Raycasting extension creates 3D rendered versions of tiles on the tilemap and shifts the camera to the perspective of a sprite viewing tiles as 3-dimensional blocks. It creates an engaging visual experience for the user that is very different from the top down tilemap!
steps.instructions:
Begin by exploring the existing project.


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap on screen. Use the direction buttons to move the Player sprite around the screen. Overlap the Key sprite, then unlock the museum to collect all 5 Artifact sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you notice how the left and right direction buttons change the horizontal angle and direction of movement, and how the up and down direction buttons move the player forwards and backwards?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the 3D perspective change the User Experience (UX) of the game?

❓ Why is a sprite image not needed for the Player sprite?

❓ How does the user move the Player sprite around the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getRenderSpriteVariable function renders a 3D view of the tilemap from the sprite’s perspective. This means that this draws a traditional tilemap game into a “3D view”, where the tiles have height, instead of appearing flat on the screen. Additionally, the user cannot see the Player sprite because the camera is shown from the Player’s point of view. This means that a sprite image is not required for the sprite that is 3D rendered.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the Player sprite’s movement in the 3D tilemap view. Prompt the ninja to notice what feels similar and what feels different about the camera and movement, as compared to the top down tilemap view.
steps.instructions:
Use the Raycasting extension to see the tilemap from a 3D perspective!


Click Extensions then scroll down to add the raycasting extension to the project.


Open 3D Render and drag [myself sprite] underneath // player sprite. Notice how the code blocks turns into JavaScript text: 

let mySprite = Render.getRenderSpriteVariable()

The getRenderSpriteVariable function renders a 3D view of the tilemap from the sprite’s perspective. The camera becomes the point of view of a sprite viewing tiles as 3-dimensional blocks, instead of a top down view. 


Name the rendered sprite player. Delete the existing code that creates a Player sprite. Because the getRenderSpriteVariable function has its own movement and camera views, the moveSprite and cameraFollowSprite functions can also be deleted.


Click ▶ to test out the project and notice how the direction buttons work differently in a 3D view.

steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed? 

❓ Why might it be useful to toggle between 2 different views in the project? 

❓ How is the sprite’s movement different in the top down versus 3D tilemap views?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is pressed, the sprite’s view switches between the default top down tilemap view and the 3D tilemap view.

💡 It’s useful to place the toggleViewMode function inside an on button pressed event to allow the user to control their view of the project. This also enables the button to be pressed multiple times, rather than a set time during the project. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that when they switch back to the default top down tilemap view, a teal square with a red dial appears on the screen. This is the 3D rendered sprite, as viewed on the top down tilemap. Encourage the ninja to test out how to move the square around the tilemap, then point out how the left and right direction buttons change the horizontal angle and direction, and the up and down direction buttons move the Player sprite forwards and backwards.
steps.instructions:
Allow the user to toggle their perspective of the tilemap between 3D and top down. 


Add a // toggle views comment, and an on A button pressed event below.


Open 3D Render and drag [toggle current view mode] into the button pressed event. Notice how the code blocks turns into JavaScript text: 

Render.toggleViewMode()

The toggleViewMode function toggles, or switches, the view between the default top down tilemap view, and the 3D view in which the tiles appear as 3-dimensional Blocks.


Click ▶ then press A to toggle between a top down and a 3D view of the tilemap.

steps.senseiHelp:

❓ Why is it important to change the background image when the tilemap perspective changes? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the A button is pressed, if topDownView is false, the variable will be set to true, the topDownBackground asset will be displayed on screen, and the view will be toggled. Else, the variable will be set to false, the 3DBackgroundOutside asset will be displayed on screen, and the view will be toggled.

💡 Point out to the ninja that it’s important to change the background image when the tilemap perspective changes because it affects and improves the User Experience (UX) in the project. The ninja should aim to make their project feel as realistic as possible. In a top down tilemap, the user should only be able to see the floor because of their perspective. In a 3D tilemap, because the user views the tilemap from the side, they should be able to see the floor and the ceiling (or the sky).
